overview.title: A medina that still feels lived-in
overview.p1: Tetouan’s medina is compact compared with Fez, whitewashed and full of workshops. Leather, textiles and small food stalls sit beside residential lanes. Spanish influence shows in the street rhythm and in how people move between square and souk.
overview.p2: Start from Place Hassan II, pick one main axis, and let side streets pull you in. You will get lost once — that is normal. The square is your reset button.
overview.p3: Morning light is kinder for photos and cooler for walking. Afternoons work for craft shopping when workshops are fully open.

q1.question: Is the medina easy to navigate?
q1.answer: Easier than Fez. Use Place Hassan II as your fixed point and accept one or two wrong turns.

q2.question: Do I need a guide?
q2.answer: Not required for a first look. A guide helps for workshops and history without wasted loops.

q3.question: Is bargaining expected?
q3.answer: Yes for crafts. Stay polite and ready to walk away.

q4.question: Best time of day?
q4.answer: Morning for cooler alleys; late afternoon for softer light.

q5.question: Safe at night?
q5.answer: Main lanes stay active early evening. After dark, stick to lit routes or take a taxi to your door.

food.title: Eat in the lanes
food.p1: Grills and small kitchens are the medina’s everyday food: brochettes, bread, olives and simple stews. Follow busy local tables.
food.p2: For a longer meal, riad restaurants offer patio seating a few minutes from the souks.
food.li2: Olives and spices as edible souvenirs
food.li3: Simple soup or stew at midday
food.li4: Mint tea when you need a bargaining pause

3.title: Pair with a museum
